summary:
The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency of the United Kingdom. Tynwald enacts its own statutes on gender recognition, equality and criminal law, and United Kingdom legislation reaches the island only when extended by Order in Council rather than automatically.

The Gender Recognition Act 2009 (c.11) allows transgender people to change their legal gender and to have the new gender recognised. The Equality Act 2017, granted royal assent on 18 July 2017 and largely in force from 1 January 2019, lists gender reassignment as a protected characteristic and as a ground on which discrimination is prohibited.

A ban on conversion therapy covering sexual orientation and gender identity was passed in 2020 as an amendment to the sexual offences bill in the Legislative Council and took effect in 2024. In 2024 the Isle of Man became the first British territory, and the first part of the British Isles, to prohibit the practice.

In July 2022 community consultation progressed on a hate crime bill that would explicitly include gender reassignment alongside sexual orientation and marital or civil partnership status. The bill's status after that consultation is not sourced.

Sexual offences law applies gender-neutrally. Private consensual male homosexual acts were decriminalised in September 1992 with an age of consent of twenty-one, lowered to eighteen by the Criminal Justice Act 2001 (c.4), then lowered to sixteen and made gender-neutral for all sexual conduct regardless of gender and sexual orientation by the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Act 2006 (c.3). Until 2021, Section 9 of the Sexual Offences Act 1992 retained offences of buggery and gross indecency between men if under sixteen or committed elsewhere than in private; in 2021 the more-than-two-persons specification was deleted and language on indecent exposure and sexual activity in a public place was made gender-neutral under the Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021, which received royal assent in July 2021 and took effect on 1 July 2022 by proclamation.

On partner recognition, same-sex couples have held civil partnerships since 6 April 2011 under the Civil Partnership Act 2011 (c.2), and marriage has been available since 22 July 2016 following royal assent on 19 July 2016. Existing civil partnerships could be converted without a second ceremony, and the first conversion was completed within days of entry into force. A trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex enters a jurisdiction that recognises the union.

Family law has not kept pace with that recognition. Under the Civil Partnership Act 2011, same-sex couples have had equal access to full joint or stepchild adoption since 6 April 2011 and lesbian couples have access to artificial insemination, but as of an August 2023 consultation same-sex couples are not recognised as parents on birth certificates in cases of IVF and surrogacy, and no law on the island acknowledges surrogacy.
tangentialFactors:
The primary legislative record of the island's marriage-equality debate is the Tynwald Hansard of 26 April 2016, which covers the Legislative Council's third reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 and consideration of the Equality Bill 2016.

The reform sequence is documented: Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage on 9 June 2015 and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition, the political commitment that preceded the Marriage and Civil Partnership Act in force from 22 July 2016.

The 2024 conversion-therapy prohibition places the Isle of Man ahead of every other British territory and of any other part of the British Isles on that measure, a comparison the sources state explicitly rather than a ranking derived from incident counts.
localsOnly:
Employment protection on sexual orientation predates the Equality Act 2017: the House of Keys adopted an Employment Bill amendment on 30 November 2005 protecting gay and lesbian employees from dismissal on sexual-orientation grounds, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, and the Employment Act 2006 (c.21) made dismissal on those grounds unlawful with effect from 1 September 2006.

The Equality Act 2017 lists sexual orientation as a protected characteristic and defines it to include attraction to the same, opposite or either sex and lack of attraction to either sex.

The Sexual Offences and Obscene Publications Act 2021 pardoned historical gay sex offences committed before 1992, explicitly modelled on the United Kingdom's Alan Turing law of 2017. Chief Minister Howard Quayle issued an unqualified apology to gay men convicted under previous laws, and in August 2022, on the thirtieth anniversary of decriminalisation, the police commissioner formally apologised for enforcement of anti-gay laws up to 1992.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Isle of Man Prison at Jurby, the island's only functioning prison, became fully operational on 14 August 2008 and is operated by the Isle of Man Prison Service, with separate units for remand and convicted prisoners, female prisoners, young offenders and vulnerable prisoners, plus a segregation unit. No birth-sex-versus-identity placement rule, no trans-specific unit and no trans-specific solitary or segregation practice are documented; the prison-housing axis therefore yields no usable finding.

The status of the hate crime bill after the July 2022 community consultation is unresolved in the sources, as is any update to the birth-certificate position for IVF and surrogacy after the August 2023 consultation.

No trans-specific violence or killing figures are sourced for the Isle of Man, so no comparison with the island's general homicide rate can be made.
